prompt: Cyanide forms linear M–CN–M' bridges. What kind of network results when cyanide links octahedral metal centers, as in Prussian blue?

choices.text: A cubic three-dimensional network
A two-dimensional network of interlinked squares
choices.why: That forms when square planar centers are linked, as in Hofmann clathrates.

choices.text: Isolated linear chains
choices.why: Octahedral centers have bonds along x, y, and z, so linear bridges connect them in all three directions.

choices.text: A hexagonal layered network
choices.why: With 90° L–M–L angles and linear bridges, the network is cubic.

explanation: When the linear cyano bridge is combined with octahedral metal centers, which have 90° L–M–L angles and bonds along the x, y, and z axes, a cubic coordination network results, as in the Prussian blue framework.

prompt: In a Hofmann clathrate, square planar [Ni(CN)4]^2− units are linked into a network. What is its overall structure?

choices.text: Two-dimensional layers of interlinked squares, with guest molecules between the layers
A cubic three-dimensional framework like Prussian blue
choices.why: Square planar centers point their bonds in only one plane, so they give 2D layers, not a cubic network.

choices.text: Discrete molecular cages with no extended structure
choices.why: The cyanide bridges link the units into extended layers.

choices.text: Linear chains of single nickel atoms
choices.why: Each square planar unit links in four directions in a plane, giving sheets.

explanation: A square planar metal center gives a 2D network of interlinked squares instead of a cubic one. In the Hofmann clathrate, square planar [Ni(CN)4]^2− units are linked by trans-Ni(NH3)2^2+ units into layers; water sits between the layers, and similar structures can adjust to hold a variety of organic molecules.

prompt: In idealized Prussian blue, Fe^3+ ions and [Fe^II(CN)6]^4− units form a neutral framework. How many Fe^3+ ions are needed to balance the charge of three [Fe^II(CN)6]^4− units?
explanation: Three [Fe(CN)6]^4− units carry 3 × (−4) = −12. Balancing that with Fe^3+ takes 12 ÷ 3 = 4 ions, giving Fe4[Fe(CN)6]3, a 4:3 ratio. Because of that ratio, some [Fe(CN)6]^4− sites in the cubic framework are not occupied by ferrocyanide.

prompt: Why is it possible to design metal complexes and organic linkers as building blocks for coordination polyhedra and networks?

choices.text: Metal–ligand bonds point in well-characterized, predictable directions set by the coordination geometry
Metal–ligand bonds are nondirectional, like ionic bonds
choices.why: The design approach depends on M–L bonds having predictable directions.

choices.text: Any metal will bond to any linker at any angle
choices.why: Building-block design works because the angles are fixed by the metal's geometry and the linker's shape.

choices.text: Organic linkers determine the structure, regardless of metal geometry
choices.why: Both matter: the structure depends on the geometry of the metal centers, the ligand, and the bonds formed.

explanation: The structure formed when bridging ligands link metals depends on the geometry of the metal centers, the ligand, and the M–L bonds. Because the directionality of metal–ligand bonding is well characterized, metal complexes with substitutable sites in defined directions can be combined with linkers whose binding sites point in defined directions.

prompt: Lehn's molecular trigonal prism relied on a geometric fact about tetrahedral bis-chelates. What is it?

choices.text: Two planar bidentate ligands on a tetrahedral metal center are oriented perpendicular (90°) to each other
Two planar bidentate ligands on a tetrahedral center lie in the same plane
choices.why: In a tetrahedral bis-chelate the two chelate planes are perpendicular, not coplanar.

choices.text: Tetrahedral centers can bind only one bidentate ligand
choices.why: A tetrahedral center can bind two bidentate ligands; their perpendicular orientation was the key.

choices.text: Tetrahedral bis-chelates are always square planar
choices.why: A tetrahedral center keeps its tetrahedral geometry, which sets the two chelates at 90°.

explanation: Lehn recognized that planar bidentate ligands in a tetrahedral bis-chelate are oriented perpendicular to each other. Combining such metal centers with rigid trigonal planar and linear nitrogen-donor linkers that bind in bidentate fashion gave a molecular trigonal prism.

prompt: What is a metal organic framework (MOF)?

choices.text: A porous coordination polymer in which metal building units are linked by rigid organic ligands
A dense ionic solid with no internal voids
choices.why: MOFs are porous, with open voids that can hold small molecules.

choices.text: An aluminosilicate mineral
choices.why: Zeolites are aluminosilicates. MOFs have porous structures similar to zeolites but are built from metals and organic linkers.

choices.text: A single discrete metal complex dissolved in an organic solvent
choices.why: MOFs are extended network solids, not discrete molecules.

explanation: MOFs consist of metal centers linked by rigid organic ligands into a porous structure similar to aluminosilicate zeolites. Their voids can hold small molecules, which is why MOFs are of interest for storing and separating gases.

prompt: In MOFs built from carboxylate linkers, why does each carboxylate usually bind κ^1 to two different metal centers?

choices.text: Single-metal κ^1 binding is too flexible for a rigid network, and κ^2 chelation forms small, less stable rings
Carboxylates can only bind through carbon
choices.why: Carboxylates bind through their oxygen atoms; here each O binds a different metal.

choices.text: κ^2 chelation to one metal is always the most stable mode
choices.why: The small chelate rings and narrow bite angles of κ^2 binding make it less stable.

choices.text: Bridging makes the network more flexible
choices.why: Bridging two metals is what makes the network rigid.

explanation: Carboxylate groups in MOFs commonly bind κ^1 to two different metals. Binding κ^1 to a single metal is too flexible to give rigid networks, while κ^2 chelation forms small rings with narrow bite angles that are less stable. This bridging mode needs metal building blocks with two or more metals held close together.

prompt: A paddlewheel carboxylate secondary building unit (SBU) has two metals spanned by carboxylate ligands in a square planar arrangement. How many carboxylate ligands bridge the two metals?
explanation: A paddlewheel SBU consists of two metals spanned by a square plane of four carboxylates. Axial sites perpendicular to the carboxylates may hold extra ligands or be left open.

prompt: The basic zinc acetate SBU used in MOF-5 has a central O^2− surrounded by a tetrahedron of four Zn^2+ ions. What is the charge on the Zn4O core?
explanation: 4 × (+2) + (−2) = +6, so the core is Zn4O^6+. Six carboxylates spanning the tetrahedron's six edges balance this charge and point toward the vertices of an octahedron.

prompt: How can the pore size of a MOF-5-type framework be increased?

choices.text: Use a longer organic linker, such as one with more benzene rings
Use a smaller metal ion
choices.why: The spacing between the Zn4O nodes, and so the pore size, is set by the length of the organic linker.

choices.text: Remove the Zn4O nodes
choices.why: Without the metal nodes there is no framework. The linkers set the spacing between them.

choices.text: Replace the linear linker with a shorter one
choices.why: Shorter linkers bring the nodes closer and make the pores smaller.

explanation: In MOF-5, Zn4O^6+ pseudooctahedra are linked by linear terephthalate (1,4-benzenedicarboxylate) ligands. The size of the cubic unit cell, and so the pores, depends on the length of the organic part of the linker; using linkers with two or three benzene rings instead of one makes the pores larger.
